'''Derrick Vincent Thomas''' (January 1, 1967 – February 8, 2000) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[linebacker]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Nicknamed "'''D. T.'''", he played 11 seasons with the Chiefs until his death in 2000. He is considered one of the greatest [[pass rush]]ers of all time.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/nflnetwork/story?id=09000d5d8088a0ec&template=with-video&confirm=true|title=Top 10 pass rushers in NFL history|date=October 7, 2008|work=NFL.com|access-date=February 1, 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090206011446/http://www.nfl.com/nflnetwork/story?id=09000d5d8088a0ec&template=with-video&confirm=true|archive-date=February 6, 2009}}</ref>

Thomas played [[college football]] for the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama Crimson Tide]], winning the [[Butkus Award]] in 1988. He was selected fourth overall in the [[1989 NFL draft]] by the Chiefs, where he received nine [[Pro Bowl]] and two first-team [[All-Pro]] selections. Thomas also set the single-game sacks record in 1990.

After the Chiefs' 1999 season, Thomas was rendered [[paraplegia|paraplegic]] in a car crash and died two weeks later from a [[pulmonary embolism]]. He was posthumously inducted to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2009 and the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2014.

'''Derrick O'Hara Johnson''' (born November 22, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]], twice earning consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors. Johnson was selected by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the first round of the [[2005 NFL draft]] with the 15th overall pick. In his 13 seasons with the Chiefs, Johnson made four [[Pro Bowl]]s. He also played six games for the [[Oakland Raiders]] in 2018.

'''Derrick James Mason''' (born January 17, 1974) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for fifteen seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Michigan State Spartans football|Michigan State Spartans]] and was selected in the fourth round of the [[1997 NFL draft]] by the [[Tennessee Oilers]] (which was renamed the Titans in 1999). After eight seasons with Tennessee, Mason signed with the [[Baltimore Ravens]], becoming the franchise's all-time leading receiver with 5,777 yards from 2005 to 2010. He spent 2011 with the [[New York Jets]] and [[Houston Texans]] before retiring as a Raven on June 11, 2012.

A two-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection ([[2001 Pro Bowl|2000]], [[2004 Pro Bowl|2003]]) and First Team [[All-Pro]] selection ([[2000 All-Pro Team|2000]]), Mason is the only player in NFL history with at least 10,000 receiving yards and 5,000 return yards.<ref name="CBSbaltimore">{{Cite web |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/baltimore/news/derrick-mason-with-a-former-players-perspective-on-the-ravens-draft/ |title=Derrick Mason With A Former Player's Perspective On The Ravens Draft |website=cbsnews.com |date= May 13, 2014 |access-date=July 21, 2025}}</ref> He set the record for all-purpose yards in a single season, which was later broken by [[Darren Sproles]].<ref name=bell/> At the time of his retirement, Mason was the last active NFL player to have played for the Oilers before the franchise's rebranding.

'''Derrick Lewis''' (born October 30, 1975) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[San Diego State Aztecs football|San Diego State Aztecs]].

He was signed as an [[undrafted free agent]] in [[2002 NFL season|2002]] with the [[New Orleans Saints]] and spent two years with the Saints before spending two years with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]]. He signed with the [[Houston Texans]] as a [[free agent]] in 2006. The spring before, Lewis started as an [[offensive specialist]] for the Arena Football League's Austin Wranglers. While a Wrangler, Lewis broke the record for single-season receptions, in addition to being considered by many a beneficial component for the Wranglers' first ever playoff berth in franchise history. Lewis played his first year of organized [[College football|football]] at [[Sacramento City College]] in 1998 and caught 34 passes. He transferred to [[San Diego State University]] in 1999.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/north-county-times-san-diego-state-signs/149934638/ |title=San Diego State signs five CC players |newspaper=[[North County Times]] |page=18 |date=1999-01-05 |access-date=2024-06-23 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

'''Derrick Wimbush''' (born August 26, 1980) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Fort Valley State Wildcats football|Fort Valley State Wildcats]] in [[Fort Valley, Georgia]]. Wimbush finished his senior season with 1,840 rushing yards and 22 touchdowns and his career with 3,188 rushing yards. Wimbush was runner up for the 2004 [[Harlon Hill Trophy]] given to best player in [[NCAA Division II]]. During his brief career with the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], Wimbush rarely carried the ball, however his blocking, and his play on special teams has contributed to a highly skilled, rushing attack from the Jaguars. In 2016, Wimbush signed with the [[Georgia Firebirds]] of [[American Indoor Football]] (AIF).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oursportscentral.com/services/releases/firebirds-add-four-to-roster/n-5117812 |title=Firebirds Add Four to Roster |date=April 1, 2016 |publisher=OurSports Central |work=www.oursportscentral.com |accessdate=April 18, 2016}}</ref> He also played for the [[Georgia Firebirds]] of the [[National Arena League]] (NAL).<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nationalarenaleague.com/rosters/georgia-firebirds.html?site=1 | title=Georgia Firebirds | publisher=nationalarenaleague.com | accessdate=December 13, 2016 | url-status=bot: unknown | archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20161214023421/http://www.nationalarenaleague.com/rosters/georgia-firebirds.html?site=1 | archivedate=December 14, 2016 }}</ref>

'''Derrick Kent Ramsey''' (born December 23, 1956) is an American administrator and former professional [[American football|football]] player. He played as a [[tight end]] for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). After his football career, he was Kentucky Secretary of Education and Workforce Development in 2018 and 2019,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Former NFL player Derrick Ramsey appointed new secretary |url=https://newpittsburghcourieronline.com/2018/06/17/former-nfl-player-derrick-ramsey-appointed-new-secretary/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180706190752/https://newpittsburghcourieronline.com/2018/06/17/former-nfl-player-derrick-ramsey-appointed-new-secretary/ |archive-date=July 6, 2018 |access-date=July 6, 2018 |website=New Pittsburgh Courier}}</ref> under [[Governor of Kentucky|Governor]] [[Matt Bevin]], after serving as secretary of the Labor Cabinet from 2015 to 2018.<ref name=seclabor>{{cite news |title=Derrick Ramsey to head Labor Cabinet under Bevin |agency=Associated Press State Wire |date=December 2, 2015}}</ref> He served as Deputy Secretary of Commerce under another Republican governor, [[Ernie Fletcher]], from 2003 to 2007.<ref name=seclabor /> Bevin appointed him to the Board of Trustees of University of Kentucky on July 25, 2017. He served until 2023.<ref>{{cite web |title=Derrick K. Ramsey |url=https://www.uky.edu/trustees/members/derrick-k.-ramsey |website=uky.edu}}</ref> He was a senior fellow at [[The Urban Institute]], then a senior fellow at the Kentucky Community and Technical College System, leading projects for the chancellor and president. In January 2024, Ramsey became special assistant to KCTCS President [[Ryan Quarles]] for strategic partnerships.<ref>Paducah Sun, Jan. 24, 2024</ref> Quarles had placed second in the 2023 Republican primary for governor.

He grew up in [[Hastings, Florida]] and attended [[Hastings High School (Florida)|Hastings High School]], where he won state football championships in his first two years. He moved to live with an uncle in [[Camden, New Jersey]], and play for the [[Camden High School (New Jersey)|Camden High School]] football team, which went 2–8 in his junior year and won the New Jersey state championship in his senior year.<ref>Hitchner, Emelia. [https://www.staugustine.com/news/local-news/2016-06-26/big-man-small-town "Catching up with a hometown hero"], ''[[The St. Augustine Record]]'', June 26, 2016. Accessed July 25, 2019. "'By going to Camden, we thought that opportunity would be afforded to me,' Ramsey said. 'And it was.' While playing at Camden High School, Ramsey added another high school football championship to his resume in 1974."</ref>

Ramsey attended the [[University of Kentucky]], where he played [[college football]] for the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky Wildcats]] as a [[quarterback]] and [[tight end]]. He was part of the team that won the 1976 SEC championship and the 1976 [[1976 Peach Bowl|Peach Bowl]].<ref>[http://www.ukathletics.com/index.php?s=&url_channel_id=39&url_article_id=7166&change_well_id=2 ukathletics.com - Kentucky Football History and Records] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070701103431/http://www.ukathletics.com/index.php?s=&url_channel_id=39&url_article_id=7166&change_well_id=2 |date=July 1, 2007 }}</ref>  He was first-team [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-SEC]] and third-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] as quarterback in 1977, when Kentucky finished with a 10–1 record and No. 6 ranking in the final [[AP poll]].   Ramsey also played two games on the [[Kentucky Wildcats men's basketball|Wildcats basketball team]] as a [[Walk-on (sports)|walk-on]] in 1976.<ref name=bbh>{{cite web|title=Derrick Ramsey|url=http://www.bigbluehistory.net/bb/Statistics/Players/Ramsey_Derrick.html|publisher=BigBlueHistory.net|access-date=March 4, 2012}}</ref> He played in the NFL for the [[Oakland Raiders|Oakland/Los Angeles Raiders]], [[New England Patriots]], and [[Detroit Lions]].

He has a master's degree in sports administration from [[Eastern Kentucky University]] and served as the [[Athletic Director]] at [[Coppin State University]] from 2008 to 2015.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.coppinstatesports.com/staff.aspx?staff=1 |title=Coppin State Athletic Department |date=July 26, 2011 |access-date=March 30, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402103415/http://www.coppinstatesports.com/staff.aspx?staff=1 |archive-date=April 2, 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

'''Derrick Todd Harmon''' (born April 26, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who played [[running back]] for the [[San Francisco 49ers]] from 1984 to 1986.

Harmon played [[college football]] at [[Cornell University]], where he still holds numerous records. He was a two-time Academic All-American, a member of the Associated Press Division I-AA All-America second-team, and a two-time member of the All-Ivy first-team. He received the [[Asa Smith Bushnell III|Asa Bushnell]] Award as the [[Ivy League]] Player of the Year, and was named Cornell's first ever Sophomore of the Year in 1981 (now renamed Rookie of the Year). Harmon was the fourth person in [[Ivy League]] history to go over 1,000 yards in one season, running 1,056 yards in seven Ivy games in 1983, with his leading blocker, David Menapace.  He was voted the team's Most Valuable Player and was named the Athlete of the Year of by ''[[The Cornell Daily Sun]]'' and ''[[The Ithaca Journal]]''. Harmon graduated as an engineering physics major in 1984 and was a member of the [[Quill and Dagger]] society.<ref>[http://www.cornellbigred.com/Pdfs/football/2007/7/10/67-108.pdf 2007 Cornell University Football Media Guide History and Records]</ref>

In 1984, Harmon was drafted to the [[National Football League]] in the ninth round by the [[San Francisco 49ers]]. It was not until 1997 that another Cornellian was drafted by the [[NFL]]. He played in the [[Super Bowl XIX]] win against the [[Miami Dolphins]] in 1985 and was the first alumnus of [[Cornell University]] to win a [[Super Bowl]] ring.

Harmon was inducted into the [[Cornell University]] Athletic Hall of Fame in 1989.<ref>[http://www.cornellbigred.com/hof.aspx?hid=2727 Cornell University Athletic Hall of Fame]</ref> He is the brother of [[NFL]] players [[Ronnie Harmon]] and [[Kevin Harmon]].
Derrick was an engineering student and later pursued a career in academics.

'''Sidney Derrick Harris''' (born September 18, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for four seasons with the [[St. Louis Rams]] and [[San Diego Chargers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). (New England came back, tying the game in the final minute and then winning in [[Overtime (sports)|overtime]]. The game marked the first come from behind win in [[Tom Brady]]'s career, but the blocked punt, and his reaction to it, resulted in [[Punter (American football)|punter]] [[Lee Johnson (punter)|Lee Johnson]]'s release following the game.  Just four games earlier, Johnson had become the all-time leader in punting yardage, a feat made possible by some inferior [[Cincinnati Bengals]] and New England Patriots offenses over the course of Johnson's career.) Nicknamed "'''King Henry'''",<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sobleski |first=Brent |date=October 19, 2021 |title=In QB-Obsessed NFL, 'King' Derrick Henry Is Making the Case to Sit on MVP Throne |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2949531-in-qb-obsessed-nfl-king-derrick-henry-is-making-the-case-to-sit-on-mvp-throne |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211026190814/https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2949531-in-qb-obsessed-nfl-king-derrick-henry-is-making-the-case-to-sit-on-mvp-throne |archive-date=October 26, 2021 |access-date=October 26, 2021 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Dunlap |first=Ryan |date=April 1, 2021 |title=HANG™ with Derrick Henry |url=https://hangtn.com/collections/have-a-nice-game-with-derrick-henry |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210413110246/https://hangtn.com/collections/derrick-henry-x-hang-tn |archive-date=April 13, 2021 |access-date=April 13, 2021 |website=Have A Nice Game |language=en}}</ref> he is known for his imposing style of play and larger build than the average running back. Noted for his success at every stage of his career, Henry is the only player to have rushed for at least 2,000 yards in a season at the high school, college, and professional levels.<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |last=Mathur|first=Ashish|date=August 3, 2023|title=Titans' Derrick Henry Is Only Running Back In Football History To Do This|url=https://nflanalysis.net/nfl-news-rumors-derrick-henry-history-tennessee-titans/|access-date=February 2, 2025|website=NFL Analysis Network|language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250426115804/https://nflanalysis.net/nfl-news-rumors-derrick-henry-history-tennessee-titans/|archive-date=April 26, 2025}}</ref> He also led the nation in rushing yards and rushing touchdowns at all three levels.

Born and raised in [[Yulee, Florida]], Henry set the national [[high school football]] record for career rushing yards with the [[Yulee High School|Yulee Hornets]], breaking [[Ken Hall (American football)|Ken Hall]]'s record that had stood for almost 60 years. Henry was a five star recruit according to [[ESPN]].<ref name=":21" /> He played [[college football]] for the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama Crimson Tide]], where during his junior season, he broke [[Herschel Walker]]'s single-season college rushing yards record in the [[Southeastern Conference]] (SEC), won the 2015 [[Heisman Trophy]], the [[Doak Walker Award]], the [[Maxwell Award]], and the [[Walter Camp Award]], and was a key part of the [[2015 Alabama Crimson Tide football team]] that won the [[2016 College Football Playoff National Championship]].

Henry was selected by the [[Tennessee Titans]] in the second round of the [[2016 NFL draft]], where he was a four-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection.<ref name="JohnTalty">{{Cite web |last=Talty |first=John |date=April 30, 2016 |title=Tennessee Titans draft Derrick Henry in second round |url=https://www.al.com/alabamafootball/2016/04/draft_derrick_henry.html |access-date=February 25, 2025 |website=AL.com |language=en}}</ref> A backup for most of his first two seasons in the league, Henry emerged as the Titans' feature back near the end of the [[2018 Tennessee Titans season|2018 season]]. He [[List of National Football League annual rushing yards leaders|led the NFL in rushing yards]] for the [[2019 NFL season|2019 season]], as well as [[List of National Football League annual rushing touchdowns leaders|rushing touchdowns]] (tied with [[2019 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] running back [[Aaron Jones (running back)|Aaron Jones]]). In 2020, Henry again led the league in both rushing yards and rushing touchdowns, becoming just the eighth player in NFL history—and the second Tennessee Titan after [[Chris Johnson (running back)|Chris Johnson]] in 2009—to surpass [[2,000-yard club|2,000 rushing yards in a single season]]. He went on to win the 2020 [[AP NFL Offensive Player of the Year|AP NFL Offensive Player of the Year Award]]. After missing more than half of the 2021 season to injury, he made his third and fourth Pro Bowl appearances in the subsequent two seasons. After eight seasons in Tennessee, Henry signed with the [[Baltimore Ravens]] in 2024, where he set multiple franchise records in his first season with the team.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sidney |first=Matt |date=December 25, 2024 |title=Derrick Henry's historic first season leaves Baltimore Ravens record books in ruins |url=https://ebonybird.com/derrick-henry-historic-first-season-leaves-baltimore-ravens-record-books-in-ruins |access-date=February 25, 2025 |website=Ebony Bird|publisher=SB Nation |language=en-us}}</ref> Through the 2025 season, Henry is the NFL's active leader in [[List of NFL career rushing yards leaders|career rushing yards]] and [[List of NFL career rushing touchdowns leaders|touchdowns]] (ranking tenth and fourth all-time, respectively).

Henry's success and dominance has also extended into the playoffs. He is the NFL's active leader in postseason rushing yards (ranking 7th all-time), holds several playoffs records, and was a key contributor to Titans' playoff wins in [[2017–18 NFL playoffs|2017–18]] and [[2019–20 NFL playoffs|2019–20]] and the Ravens' playoff win in [[2024–25 NFL playoffs|2024–25]].
